item.title: Quantum Integration Software Suite For HPC-Quantum Computing Workflows
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Introduces QASC, translating OpenQASM3.0 classical control and circuits into C++ linked to QuEST, plus QACC-perf, which estimates HPC-QPU offloading communication latencies ranging from 0.084 ms on-node to 2718.000 ms over cloud across molecular circuits up to 50.3 MB.

Grade 0.400 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Mateusz Meller, Joseph C. R. Thacker, Thomas W. Keal, Vendel Szeremi

Figure

Communication overhead in ms against circuit size in MB across on-node, multi-node, and cloud integration modes, alongside transpilation-to-execution runtime ratios across tested molecular system sizes.

Asks

How can OpenQASM3.0 programs with complex classical control be efficiently simulated and their HPC–quantum computing integration performance quantitatively modelled?

But

Does not support OpenQASM3.0 gate calibration, physical qubits, pragmas, or annotations; performance model tested via simulation rather than physical QPU hardware.

Tools

QASC (Quantum Assembly Compiler) · QuEST simulator · QACC-perf performance model · ChemShell · Antlr4

Code. https://github.com/stfc/QASC

Abstract

In this work, we focus on addressing challenges related to modelling the integration of conventional high-performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing (QC). We introduce the Quantum Assembly Compiler (QASC) for OpenQASM3.0 files. The compiler produces an executable that leverages the high-performance simulator QuEST to simulate quantum programs. Additionally, we introduce a performance modelling tool, QACC-perf, which can estimate the cost of integrating QC in classical HPC workflows, as well as the execution time of the quantum circuits. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these tools in the context of multiscale quantum chemistry workflows using the ChemShell computational chemistry environment.

item.title: Entanglement in Collective Neutrino Oscillations on a Quantum Computer
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Multiparticle neutrino oscillations converge to Boltzmann-type mean-field kinetic solutions as particle number N grows, with RMS residuals declining towards zero up to N=1300000. Mean-field breakdown requires non-mean-field conditions like linear streams with overlapping wave packets or chained once-in-a-lifetime encounters.

Grade 0.392 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum simulations with ultracold quantum gases” · Katarina Bleau, Nikolina Ilic, Joachim Kopp, Ushak Rahaman, Xin Yue Yu

Figure

Flavor survival probability vs. dimensionless time and root-mean-square residuals vs. particle number per mode N. Demonstrates convergence of full multiparticle classical and quantum processor simulations to the quantum kinetic mean-field limit as N increases.

Asks

Does quantum entanglement survive to invalidate mean-field quantum kinetic equations for collective neutrino oscillations in dense astrophysical environments as the number of neutrinos grows large?

But

Demonstrated analytically and numerically on two-mode toy systems (electron-muon and neutrino-antineutrino bipolar oscillations); full astrophysical environments are three-dimensional, turbulent, and multi-scale.

Tools

superconducting transmon quantum processor · Trotterized quantum simulation circuit with Draper adder · adaptive dynamic truncation classical algorithm · Clebsch-Gordan angular momentum decomposition

Abstract

Simulations on a quantum computer have been propounded as a next-generation tool for studying neutrino flavour oscillations in dense environments like supernovae or neutron star mergers. However, quantum advantage hinges on the presence of quantum entanglement in the neutrino ensemble, and it has been argued that such entanglement becomes negligible in the limit of large neutrino number density. Here, we address this question by explicitly simulating the multiparticle dynamics of entangled neutrino ensembles with a varying number of particles, N, on both classical and quantum hardware, and comparing our results to those obtained with conventional ``mean-field'' methods based on Boltzmann-type kinetic equations. For simple toy systems, we demonstrate both analytically and numerically that, indeed, the predictions of full multiparticle simulations agree with those of mean-field methods in the large-N limit. Along the way, we develop novel algorithms for the efficient simulation of entangled neutrino gases on both classical and quantum hardware. We then discuss physical situations in which an entangled neutrino system emphcannot be described through mean-field dynamics alone and quantum entanglement therefore becomes phenomenologically relevant. We comment on the conditions under which these scenarios may be realized in supernova cores or neutron star mergers.

item.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Discovers and formally verifies quantum circuits across 5 benchmarks, lowering logical spacetime volume Q⋅𝒯 up to 290x for arithmetic and 2.5x to 11x for large-scale scientific simulations.

Grade 0.386 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, Francisco J. H. Heras, Nicholas C. Rubin, Guang Hao Low, Sébastien Racanière, Nenad Tomavsev, Lei M. Zhang, James Watson, Tanuj Khattar, Aws Albarghouthi, Stavan Jain, Harun Khan, Leopoldo Sarra, Andrew W. Senior, Michael Broughton, Hussain Masoom, Sergio Boixo, Ryan Babbush, Swarat Chaudhuri, Pushmeet Kohli

Figure

Resource costs for quantum algorithms across applications comparing prior baselines against verified discovered circuits, showing logical qubit and T-gate reductions.

Asks

Can multi-agent LLM systems automatically discover and formally verify resource-reduced quantum algorithms at scales beyond classical simulation?

Before

For cytochrome P450, prior compiled baseline was Qbase⋅𝒯base=1.09×1012 (Q=481, 𝒯=2.26×109).

But

Circuits and proofs target fault-tolerant architectures counting logical qubits and T gates (Q⋅𝒯); assumes idealized clean ancilla reset and exact/bounded-error synthesis without physical noise models.

Tools

Lean 4 interactive theorem prover · Quantum Hoare logic (QHL) · LLM multi-agent collaborative framework · One-hot Givens rotation synthesis

Abstract

The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

item.title: A Complete Calculus for Hamiltonian Quantum Programming
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Introduced Hamilton, a process calculus for Hamiltonian quantum computing. Semantics is fully abstract, equational theory is complete and decidable, and expressible Hamiltonians are precisely those with dyadic rational Pauli coefficients m/2k.

Grade 0.385 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “lattice gauge theory simulation on quantum hardware” · Jacques Carette, Chris Heunen, Robin Kaarsgaard, Neil J. Ross, Amr Sabry

Figure

Survival probability |a3(t)|2 of a proton in a hydrogen bond at state |11⟩ over time t up to 40 fs. Refined compiled circuits at n=4 track the exact continuous Hamiltonian evolution with maximum deviation ≤0.0042.

Asks

Can quantum programming treat continuous Hamiltonian evolution as an additive concurrent primitive with a sound, complete, and fully abstract equational calculus?

Before

Circuit-level equational reasoning (like ZX phase gadgets or Πk) handles unitaries at fixed precision but lacks an equational theory complete for Hamiltonians and their additive combinations.

But

Only targets first-order Lie-Trotter splittings; circuit emissions lack multi-qubit resynthesis/optimization (e.g. 18 CNOTs per step instead of 3); purely unitary with no dissipative dynamics, mid-circuit measurement, or block encoding.

Tools

Lie-Trotter product formula · Π_k quantum circuit calculus · concurrent process algebra · Agda formal proof verification

Abstract

Given the forces acting on a quantum particle, a Hamiltonian models its continuous evolution. Quantum computers evolve Hamiltonians to simulate physical systems, to solve optimisation problems, and to estimate eigenvalues, and even the popular circuit abstraction is compiled to Hamiltonians on the hardware. We introduce Hamilton, a process calculus whose parallel operator is the sum of interactions acting simultaneously. Its operational semantics is the Lie-Trotter product formula, which recovers a sum as the limit of ever finer sequential interleavings; compiling a program means halving it to a chosen precision and unrolling the interleaving into a circuit. The semantics is fully abstract, the expressible Hamiltonians are exactly those whose Pauli coefficients have the form m/2^k, the precision that successive halving reaches, and the equational theory is complete and decidable. A full implementation compiles Hamilton programs to circuits and decides their equivalence, and Agda proofs sanity-check the core metatheory.

item.title: Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of 1.11(30)×10−3 and achieving quantum volume of 24=16 with 83.1% mean heavy-output probability.

Grade 0.379 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Marco Rossignolo, Lorena C. Bianchet, Anurag Saha Roy, Shai Machnes

Figure

Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at 83.1%, exceeding the 2/3 pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.

Asks

How can atomic quantum processor dynamics and hardware control stacks be modelled and calibrated using end-to-end automatic differentiation?

But

Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.

Tools

automatic differentiation · quantum optimal control · digital twin modeling · Qiskit backend emulation · randomized benchmarking

Abstract

Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.

item.title: Lefschetz-Thimble Method to the Sign Problem in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Model
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Complex Langevin search combined with Lefschetz-thimble Monte Carlo integration reproduces the high-temperature partition function and imaginary-time Green function G(τ) of the four-body SYK model. Path integral weight is heavily concentrated near the real axis, with the origin contributing about 2.3% of the average real weight while complex saddle points fall to order 10−4.

Grade 0.349 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Yin-Hao Fang, Yang Qi

Figure

Imaginary-time Green function G(τ) plotted against τ at β=1, N=16, and Nτ=16. Compares continuous Lefschetz-thimble Monte Carlo integration, sign-reweighted discrete DQMC, and infrared-limit theoretical curves across three values of coupling J.

Asks

Can complex Langevin dynamics correctly locate all contributing saddle points and evaluate the Lefschetz-thimble path integral for the sign-problematic Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model?

But

Statistically equivalent representation of four-body SYK rather than identical Hamiltonian; tested up to N=32 fermions and Nτ=16 time slices; importance sampling truncates at weight e−18.

Tools

Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation · complex Langevin equation · Lefschetz-thimble gradient flow · Pfaffian evaluation · discrete DQMC with sign reweighting

Abstract

The sign problem in path integrals severely limits the application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to strongly correlated systems, whereas the Lefschetz-thimble method offers a rigorous framework to mitigate this issue. In this paper, we establish a numerical framework based on the Lefschetz thimbles for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model. By introducing continuous auxiliary fields via the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, the partition function is formulated as a high-dimensional complex integral. We employ the complex Langevin equation to explore the saddle-point distribution of the effective action in the complex plane. Monte Carlo integration is then performed to compute the partition function and Green functions. Our numerical results exhibit excellent agreement with high-temperature expansions, infrared-limit solutions, and determinantal quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations, confirming the validity of our framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our complex Langevin search successfully captures the relevant dominant saddle points governing the SYK model in the large-N limit. Our work deepens the understanding of the sign problem in the SYK model and provides a viable non-perturbative avenue for addressing sign problems in more complex strongly correlated systems.

item.title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
item.description:
Worth a look new result — The universal lower bound 4ℱA≤ℳlinNL holds across >260 nuclei and approaches saturation for weakly entangled states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit distinct quantum complexity patterns compared to even-even and odd-even systems, showing elevated non-local magic alongside low entanglement spectrum antiflatness.

Grade 0.340 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · James W. T. Keeble, Caroline E. P. Robin, Federico Rocco, Martin J. Savage

Figure

Non-local linear magic ℳlinNL versus 4ℱA across >260 nuclei; all points lie above the equality line 4ℱA=ℳlinNL, with odd-odd nuclei showing distinct elevation above the bound.

Asks

How do non-local non-stabilizerness, entanglement entropy, and entanglement spectrum antiflatness scale across nuclear ground states under a proton-neutron bipartition?

Before

Exact equality ℳlinNL=4ℱA held for two-qubit systems, and the bound was theoretically proven for general bipartitions without large-scale verification across physical nuclear states.

But

Calculations neglect isospin-breaking and electromagnetic interactions; non-local non-stabilizerness is approximated using an auxiliary Schmidt-decomposed state.

Tools

nuclear shell model · BIGSTICK Lanczos ground-state solver · Jordan-Wigner-like qubit mapping (6-44 qubits) · Markov Chain Monte Carlo Pauli sampling

Abstract

Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is challenged by the combined effects of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic). Non-local magic, M^NL_α, quantifies the component of non-stabilizerness that cannot be removed by local unitary transformations and provides a measure of quantum complexity beyond entanglement alone. It is bounded from below by the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, F_A. We calculate stabilizer Rényi entropies, non-local magic, entanglement-spectrum antiflatness, and entanglement entropy in shell-model ground states of more than 260 even-even, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei, using a bipartition into proton and neutron sectors. We find that the previously established bound 4F_A≤M^NL_lin holds for every nucleus studied and approaches saturation in the limit of separable states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit markedly different patterns of entanglement and magic compared with even-even and odd-even systems, revealing distinctive signatures of proton-neutron quantum correlations and providing new insight into the complexity generated by nuclear interactions.

item.title: Parametric CZ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulated parametric-resonance CZ gates across three pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits sharing one tunable coupler achieve target-subspace fidelities of 0.9943 (CZ01), 0.9834 (CZ02), and 0.9907 (CZ12). A spectator qubit initially in state |1⟩ suffers significant population distortion, transferring population or leaving the computational space.

Grade 0.328 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Chanpyo Kim, Hansol Kim, Jeongsoo Kang, Younghun Kwon

Figure

Population evolution of states |0110⟩, |0020⟩, and |0200⟩ over 500 ns under modulated coupler flux, demonstrating the parametric resonant interaction between |0110⟩ and |0020⟩.

Asks

Can selective parametric-resonance CZ gates be implemented between all pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler using only coupler flux modulation?

But

Numerical simulation only, with three energy levels per component and no decoherence, relaxation, dephasing, or flux noise modeled; target fidelities evaluated only on the four-state subspace where the spectator qubit and coupler remain in |0⟩.

Tools

three-level transmon Hamiltonian simulation · time-dependent flux pulse optimization · virtual Z phase correction

Abstract

Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance CZ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct CZ₀₁, CZ₀₂, and CZ₁₂ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing CZ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.
